correctness.rationale: Graph distance is Hamming distance. For q>=3 a length-d geodesic entirely in the radius-d sphere requires d+1 distinct rooted paths, meeting the diameter bound. For q=2 every edge has endpoints in adjacent root layers, allowing consecutive pairs of every geodesic to be covered one per rooted path; an alternating two-layer diametral geodesic proves the matching ceil((d+1)/2) lower bound. The d=1 endpoints are included. An exhaustive verifier checks 7,210 small-case path sets but is not used as the infinite proof.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Covering all vertices by unrestricted geodesics is not the same quantifier pattern as minimizing, over roots, the maximum number of rooted geodesics needed to cover one varying path. Thus prior global cover formulas cannot be relabeled as this claim. The present binary and q>=3 lower-bound witnesses are not corollaries of the generic upper bounds.

originality.rationale: The rooted single-geodesic invariant was defined before this result, but full-text review of the two closest foundational studies finds no exact ipco(H(d,q)) calculation. The original 2022 work cites global geodesic-cover results on Hamming products, whose statements and quantifiers differ. Neither the general diameter bound nor published class bounds implies the sharp binary value or the uniform alphabet threshold. Published-record searches and direct published-text searches reveal no covering result; unindexed historical overlap remains possible.
residual_risks: Indexed results cannot rule out unpublished or unindexed prior equivalent statements under another name.

value.rationale: A recent natural metric-graph parameter receives a full exact evaluation on all Cartesian powers of uniform complete graphs. The dichotomy between a two-layer binary zigzag and a diametral farthest-sphere path at alphabet three yields a discontinuous factor-two asymptotic change, clarifies the source of unboundedness and supplies reusable extremal geodesic witnesses. This is not a routine numerical small-graph census or rephrasing of known global isometric path covers.
